UPSTREAM: ASoC: Intel: common: filter ACPI devices with _STA return value BIOS vendors typically list multiple audio codecs in the DSDT table and enable the relevant one by changing the return value of the _STA method. With the current code, all devices are reported by acpi_dev_present(), regardless of the _STA return values. This causes errors on probe with the wrong machine driver being loaded. This patch essentially reverts 'commit 6f08cbdaac5a ("ASoC: Intel: Use acpi_dev_present()")' and adds code to force the evaluation of the _STA method. A better solution might be to make sure the ACPI subsystem only reports devices with a _STA value of 0xf but apparently it's problematic so dealing with this in the audio subsystem directly. Signed-off-by: Pierre-Louis Bossart <pierre-louis.bossart@linux.intel.com> Signed-off-by: Mark Brown <broonie@kernel.org> From v4.6-rc2 (cherry picked from commit cab473850226c3e41823453b5b80eb294dae6e0c) Signed-off-by: Vedang Patel <vedang.patel@intel.com> BUG=chrome-os-partner:53967 TEST=with the whole series applied, Audio works on Amenia. UPSTREAM: ASoC: Intel: common: add translation from HID to codec-name BIOS vendors sometimes declare multiple devices in the DSDT table that all refer to the same HID. This is not very smart but not illegal as long as only one device reports present with the _STA method. The ACPI subsystem tracks each device with an extension, e.g. 10EC5640:00 and 10EC5640:01 In the ASoC machine driver, the DAI codec name needs to refer to the ACPI device that reported present, e.g. "i2c-10EC5640:01". The extension will vary depending on how the BIOS is written and which ACPI device is activated. This patch adds a translation function that provides the codec name from the ACPI HID to avoid any hard-coded values in the machine driver. UPSTREAM: ALSA: hda - Fix unexpected resume through regmap code path HD-audio driver has a mechanism to trigger the runtime resume automatically at accessing the verbs. This auto-resume, however, causes the mutex deadlock when invoked from the regmap handler since the regmap keeps the mutex while auto-resuming. For avoiding that, there is some tricky check in the HDA regmap handler to return -EAGAIN error to back-off when the codec is powered down. Then the caller of regmap r/w will retry after properly turning on the codec power. This works in most cases, but there seems a slight race between the codec power check and the actual on-demand auto-resume trigger. This resulted in the lockdep splat, eventually leading to a real deadlock. This patch tries to address the race window by getting the runtime PM refcount at the check time using pm_runtime_get_if_in_use(). With this call, we can keep the power on only when the codec has been already turned on, and back off if not. For keeping the code consistency, the code touching the runtime PM is stored in hdac_device.c although it's used only locally in hdac_regmap.c. Reported-by: Jiri Slaby <jslaby@suse.cz> Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de> From v4.6-rc2 (cherry picked from commit fc4f000bf8c0cbf38f44de6bd5e225574e572ed4) Signed-off-by: Vedang Patel <vedang.patel@intel.com> BUG=chrome-os-partner:53967 TEST=with the whole series applied, Audio works on Amenia. UPSTREAM: mainboard: Clean up boot_option/reboot_bits in cmos.layout Since commit 3bfd7cc (drivers/pc80: Rework normal / fallback selector code) the reboot counter stored in `reboot_bits` isn't reset on a reboot with `boot_option = 1` any more. Hence, with SKIP_MAX_REBOOT_CNT_CLEAR enabled, later stages (e.g. payload, OS) have to clear the counter too, when they want to switch to normal boot. So change the bits to (h)ex instead of (r)eserved. To clarify their meaning, rename `reboot_bits` to `reboot_counter`. Also remove all occurences of the obsolete `last_boot` bit that have sneaked in again since 24391321 (mainboard: Remove last_boot NVRAM option). cryptohome: Extract attestation into dbus service child class To prepare for implementing a version of cryptohome dbus service that bounces attestation-related calls to attestationd, extract attestation-related functionality into a separate class dependant on Service and make attestation-related methods abstract in the base Service. This approach was chosen over extracting it into a separate class that can be instantiated by Service depending on the chosen attestation implementation for the following reasons: To minimize changes to the existing code, attestation methods continue to rely on Service's internal objects: mount_thread, event_source, etc. They also occasionally use tpm, tpm_init and other such objects, pointers to which are handled by Service. Giving access to it for dependant classes is more natural and less intrusive than exposing all needed internal objects to an independant class. Thus, after the two approaches (inheritance vs object encapsulation) were implemented and compared, inheritance had a more concise code and required less changes to the code that uses Service: interface, cryptohomed, unittests. CHROMIUM: arm64: dts: fake wlan_module_reset_l as a regulator It's hard to figure out a *great* place to do this, but we're supposed to wait about 8 milliseconds after enabling the supplies before taking the WiFi out of reset (7ms for ramp up and 1ms per Marvell's WiFi specification). While we could try to do this with some kind of "generic" power sequencing code (similar to what's done for SDIO in drivers/mmc/core/pwrseq.c; or what's being proposed for some USB hubs upstream, with [1]), there are a few problems: (a) sequencing code like [1] is not very generic; it codifies a very inflexible type of reset sequence, involving only a few clocks and a gpio (b) PCIe doesn't really have a nice place for handling this; all core bus code assumes devices have been powered and brought out of reset. So to use any "generic" code, we'd just have to hack it into the PCIe host driver itself anyway. It's not clear this will be very palatable upstream, and it doesn't seem to give us a lot of benefits, other than feeling good about using abstractions. So, let's do the quick/dirty/simple thing of: (1) modeling this active-low reset as an active-high regulator, whose parent supply is the 1.8v PCIe regulator (2) add an 8ms ramp delay to the parent regulator (3) pull the reset low as early as possible with a "pin control hog" (see [2]); it's currently default pull-up, and leaking current through the powered-down chip at bootup. We also want to do this as strongly as possible, to avoid fighting with the external pull up resistor. Ideally, we can get the BIOS to do #3 for us too, but this is better than nothing. [1] https://patchwork.kernel.org/patch/9267147/ [2] https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/pinctrl.txt BUG=chrome-os-partner:56069, chrome-os-partner:54026 TEST=boot kevin to wifi Change-Id: I3896096277e208c347644addfd4a4ca44155db33 Signed-off-by: Brian Norris <briannorris@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/368770 Commit-Ready: Douglas Anderson <dianders@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Douglas Anderson <dianders@chromium.org>
